title: Visualisation - US Honey Production
summary: A visualisation practice with python libraries matplotlib, seaborn
body:
**==US Honey Production: A Python Visualisation Practice Project==**

I made this project while learning Python, Pandas and data visualisation. I needed a real dataset to practise on, and the US honey production data looked simple enough to start with.

==**The dataset**==

The data is a CSV file with ++1,115 rows++ and ++9 columns++. Each row is one state in one year.

- state: the US state
- colonies_number: number of bee colonies
- yield_per_colony: average honey produced per colony
- production: total honey produced
- stocks: honey held in storage
- average_price: average selling price
- value_of_production: total value of the honey produced
- year: year of the record

## ==What I wanted to find out==

I built five charts, each answering one question.

1 Which states produce the most honey? A sorted horizontal bar chart of total production by state.

![Total production by state](assets/blog/20261107-1vyqs.webp)

2 Which states get the most honey per colony? Average yield per colony by state.

![Average yield per colony](assets/blog/20261107-lv02f.webp)

3 Where are the most colonies? Total colonies by state.

![Total colonies by state](assets/blog/20261107-a6sxl.webp)

4 Which states held the most honey stock in 2020? Stocks by state, filtered to one year.

![2020 Stock by state](assets/blog/20261107-p1hv5.webp)

5 How are the numeric columns related? A correlation heatmap made with Seaborn.

![Correlation heatmap](assets/blog/20261107-orhkp.webp)

## ==What I practised==

- Grouping and aggregating data with groupby, sum and mean, then sorting it so rankings are easy to read.

- Filtering data to a single year before aggregating.

- Picking a chart that fits the data. Horizontal bars work better for long state names, and a heatmap works for comparing many columns.

- Reading a correlation matrix and remembering that correlation does not mean one thing causes the other.

## ==Tools==

Python 3, Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn and Jupyter Notebook. The complete code is in analysis.py, and the original notebook is in the repository too.

> Peace
